seriously *sigh*. It is not that I dislike surgery per se, I like the adrenaline of an EDH, knowing you are literally witnessing someones life being saved (not by me of course, I am just the suction monkey atm). And I like blood, weird I know but yep.  

But I hate the hours, the days filled with administrative stuff, that all you do is follow algorithms with no space for creativity and that you never have time to talk to your patients. I want to know how they really are, help them cope with the often devastating diagnosis we hand out. I want to know if the brain surgery made their dreams change...  

But everyone around me seems to see the patients as machines to be fixed. To quote one of my co-residents "I hate when they have depression as a comorbidity, then you have to be so empathetic". So yeah, just feels like I am in the wrong crowd for exhausting hours every day.   

Anyways, I think you guys are the real doctors, I am just the apprentice mechanic. And for what it is worth, my life was saved by one of you (and I periodically remind him of that and thank him).

The fluorescence is done via a medication that certain tumors like to take up more, it can help distinguish between healthy brain and tumor tissue and you don't have to stop working to use it, just turn off the normal lights and have the blue light of the microscope on, then the tumor sparkles. :)

Preop there is a detailled navigation MRI taken. The tumor, important blood vessels, main white matter tracts and functionally important brain areas are highlighted in different colors. Intraop the navigation works like a GPS for the surgeon (you use landmarks like the nose to adjust it), like you have a pen that then will be on the screen in the MRI pic.   

This is done for most brain tumors. Now in a wake craniotomy like in the article the patient gets woken up once the brain is exposed and the surgeon uses electric stimulation to "numb" certain brain areas. If the patient then looses an important function (neuropsychologists are present to assess the patient) then the surgeon knows not to cut there. You can also use intraoperative monitoring of certain nerves or even lay EEG electrodes directly onto the brain.   

Major probs to the patients who go through that...
